title.en: AP Statistics Exam Format & Study Design

body.en: AP Statistics introduces students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data. The course follows four interconnected themes: Exploring Data, Sampling and Experimentation, Probability and Distributions, and Statistical Inference.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Exam Structure, Scoring & Formula Sheet

body.en: Understand the two 90-minute sections of the AP Statistics exam, scoring weights, and navigation of the official College Board formula tables.

value.en: 40 Questions · 90 min (50% of total score) · 2.25 min/question

body.en:
A student allocates 90 minutes to complete the 40 multiple-choice questions in Section I. What is the average time available per question in minutes and seconds?

Divide total time by number of questions: \[ \frac{90\text{ minutes}}{40\text{ questions}} = 2.25\text{ minutes}. \] Convert the decimal fraction of a minute to seconds: \[ 0.25 \times 60 = 15\text{ seconds} \implies \mathbf{2\text{ minutes and }15\text{ seconds per question}}. \]

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

Section II of the AP Statistics exam has 90 minutes allocated for 6 Free-Response Questions. If a student reserves 25 minutes for Question 6 (the Investigative Task), what is the exact average time available per question for Questions 1 through 5?

solution.en:
Calculate the remaining time for Questions 1 through 5: \[ 90 - 25 = 65\text{ minutes}. \]

Divide by 5 questions: \[ \frac{65\text{ minutes}}{5\text{ questions}} = \mathbf{13\text{ minutes per question}}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Investigative Task Strategy & Calculator Functions

body.en: Master the specialized calculator commands (normalcdf, invNorm, tcdf, 1-PropZTest) and learn how to tackle novel statistical reasoning in Question 6.

caption.en: AP Statistics exam score weighting across the curriculum units.

label.en: ⏱ Free Response Strategy & Question 6 Investigative Task

body.en:
• Pacing: Allot 65 minutes for Questions 1–5 (~13 minutes each) and reserve a full 25 minutes for Question 6 (the Investigative Task). Question 6 is worth 25% of your total FRQ section score!
  • Calculator & Formula Sheet: You are provided the official College Board formula sheet and statistical tables. Graphing calculators are permitted throughout the entire exam.
  • Show Statistical Notation: When writing calculator commands (like normalcdf or 1-PropZTest), always write the standard mathematical formula or label your inputs (e.g., lower, upper, mean, SD) to receive full credit.

A student needs to find the probability that a standard normal variable \(Z\) exceeds 1.75. Write the calculator syntax with labeled inputs and evaluate the probability to four decimal places.

Lower bound = 1.75, Upper bound = \(10^{99}\) (or \(\infty\)), Mean \(\mu = 0\), Standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\): \[ P(Z > 1.75) = \text{normalcdf}(\text{lower} = 1.75, \text{upper} = 10^{99}, \mu = 0, \sigma = 1) \approx \mathbf{0.0401}. \]

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Find the critical value \(z^*\) required to construct a 98% confidence interval for a population proportion, rounded to three decimal places.

solution.en:
For a 98% confidence interval, the central area is 0.98, leaving 0.02 split equally between both tails (0.01 in each tail). The area to the left of the upper critical value is: \[ 1 - 0.01 = 0.99. \]

Using the inverse normal function: \[ z^* = \text{invNorm}(0.99, 0, 1) \approx \mathbf{2.326}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — FRQ Scoring Rules, Error Analysis & Statistical Power

body.en: Apply College Board rubric standards: context in conclusions, comparative language, avoiding 'accepting H0', checking inference conditions, and analyzing Type I vs Type II errors.

label.en: ▲ The 4 Golden Rules of AP Statistics FRQs

body.en:
• 1. Always Interpret in Context: Every definition, slope, intercept, confidence interval, or conclusion MUST include the specific context (variable names, population, units). An answer with perfect numbers but missing context receives only Partial credit.
  • 2. Use Comparative Language: When comparing two distributions, never just list values for each separately. You must explicitly use comparative words: 'The median salary of Group A is greater than the median salary of Group B.'
  • 3. Never 'Accept' the Null Hypothesis: We never prove \(H_0\) is true; we only 'fail to reject \(H_0\)' due to insufficient evidence. Writing 'accept \(H_0\)' is an automatic deduction on AP rubrics.
  • 4. Check All Assumptions & Conditions: Never proceed to an inference calculation without explicitly naming and verifying the Random, 10% (independence), and Normality / Large Counts conditions.

A quality control test has \(H_0: p = 0.02\) vs \(H_a: p > 0.02\), where \(p\) is the proportion of defective microchips. Describe a Type I error, a Type II error, and state a consequence of each in context.

Type I Error: Rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true. Concluding that the defect rate is greater than 2% when it is actually at most 2%. Consequence: The company needlessly shuts down production or recalls good chips, wasting money.

Type II Error: Failing to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) is true. Concluding that the defect rate is acceptable (\(\le 2%\)) when it is actually greater than 2%. Consequence: Defective microchips are shipped to customers, damaging the company's reputation.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

An investigator conducts a hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\). Explain two distinct ways the investigator could increase the statistical power of the test without changing the true effect size.

solution.en:
1. Increase the sample size \(n\): A larger sample size reduces the standard error of the sample statistic, making the sampling distributions of \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) narrower, which increases the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis (power).

2. Increase the significance level \(\alpha\) (e.g., from 0.05 to 0.10): A larger \(\alpha\) moves the critical value closer to the center of \(H_0\), making it easier to reject \(H_0\) and thereby increasing power (at the expense of increasing the risk of a Type I error).
